whole.text: Good morning, friends and family, boys and girls, ladies and gentlemen. What kind of industry should you get into? Very basic common question I get a lot of the time. If you're already in business, stay in your lane. Sorry, let me rephrase that. If you're already in business, you're making cash, you're profitable, and you're growing, stay in your lane. If you're in business and you've been stagnant for the last 15, 20 years, I don't fucking know. Must be some deeper issues. Whether you stay in your lane, whether you change, hard to say, I'll have to find out a little bit more. If you've never been in business before, started from scratch, like say you're in my position like I was a few years ago, I go, I'm unemployed, I wanna buy companies, what do I do? Which industry do I go into? I chose healthcare. Why did I choose healthcare? Because my personality and my person naturally gravitates towards healthcare. I have a personal affinity towards good health and healthcare and societal health, the community around me. I look the part, Chinese, and I don't mind playing more towards that end of the continuum, right? When I wear the suit, when I'm a bit more sophisticated, people aren't taken back by them. Whereas if I went into more blue collar industries, the more blue collar industries, I'm not a blue collar kid. I have served many of them, or my parents have served many of them via their small businesses. And I can relate to them on that level. But I have no ambition, no passion, no juice for the other industries, all right? How did I choose healthcare? I knew it was something to do with health and boom, like I just went for it. Now, it's not to say that I didn't pivot or change. The first industry that I really wanted to get into was GPs, medical centres. Now medical centres at the time, Melbourne was under the longest lockdowns in the world. 300 and something days, 200 and something days, 256 days, I think. Anyway, the GPs were doing testing sites for the government and a lot of them were freaking out, stressed out. A lot of them just closed up shop. A lot of them weren't taking new patients. Like, it was just a whole shit store. And I couldn't really have that conversation about buying their business, especially because I didn't know what I was doing, right? So I didn't know how to navigate through the nuance. And then fast forward a little bit, I pivoted to allied health, physiotherapy. As soon as I made that pivot, fuck me. How responsive, how receptive and how much easier it was to start those conversations. My first deal was actually a call back. I went out to do a site visit at a completely different location, signed that offer. And then when I got back into the car park, just reflecting on what the fuck I just did, what I was doing. And at this time, this was the first time I met my current business partner in person. How funny, how the world works. What was I talking about? First deal, call back. Yeah, so this was off one cold email to this guy. I'm pretty sure I sent it to the head office, like the front desk email. So reception would have just got it, flicked it over to the owner. And he literally gave me a call. Literally gave me a call, said, hey, you got your email, I'm interested, what's the go? I gave him a quick one -liner and boom, boom, we're in business. Now, what does that boom, boom, we're in business. The conversation got started. Conversation got started. He was happy with my overall process and approach. It took several months to close the deal, but that was 100 % vendor finance. Didn't know what I was doing, relied on my board of directors. But I guess going back to industry, why healthcare? What made me work? What made this all work? It's not that I knew about the industry, I recruited, I hired people, I recruited people who knew more than me to help advise and govern the direction of the company. But I think my role, it is the energy, it is the passion, it is someone who's willing to fucking do the shit that no one wants to do. And that's why not a lot of people are doing, are playing the acquisitions game because it's not necessarily hard, right? Nothing's fucking hard. It is difficult and it is reserved for a particular archetype. Not to say you have to be like me, not to say you have to be extroverted, not to say you have to be, let's say, you know, loudmouth alpha extroverted, not to say that you can't make this work if you're a meanie mouse who struggles to speak up, right? It's all a learning curve, but tailor the industry, like put yourself in a position to succeed, right? So you look at the industry, I looked at healthcare, I go, well, for all the reasons I've already mentioned, I'm Chinese, I like the, you know, the aristo -sophisticated continuum rather than the casual fucking bogan continuum, right? So I went down that path. Yeah, I could have went down finance, accounting, legal firms, right? I could have went down that path. But if you're more geared towards the blue collar, the more ground work, go into that. I've got a good friend, Christian, is in Victoria. He's in waste and energy, right? The guys, the guys that he hires, they get dirty and it's the type of work, but he comes from that background, he comes from a trade background and his personality, his demeanor, it fits the picture. For some of you guys know that I learned from my virtual mentor, Dan Pena, and if you watch his material, you'll see the joke, how to pick an industry, fucking get a phone book, throw it on the ground and whatever page it lands on, just pick because you can always just pivot like I did with the GP medical centers. I went in, spent a bit too much time in that field, was getting rejected left, right and center and I felt the calling to change, to pivot, to change into a different realm, arena. So same realm, different arena. Man, it's still healthcare, right? And I'm actually glad I made that pivot because GPs and medical centers, what are they? They're just pill pushers. You go to a GP medical center, nine times out of 10, you walk away with a prescription for a drug. In physiotherapy, in allied health, we don't prescribe drugs. We prescribe natural, natural solutions, right? Like in physiotherapy, if you're injured, if you have pain, we show you how to use your body. We show you how to use your body to heal itself because that's, see the allied health, we empower the human, we empower the person whereas GPs and medical clinics, it's almost like they're fucking condescending. They're just like, oh, like, I'll go through the fucking questions, all right? Hi, yeah, any history of fucking illness, cancer, whatever, do you smoke? Do you drink? And then you'll say like, yes. And they're like, oh, no good, no good. Yeah, so you see, like if you keep drinking, but I keep smoking, blah, blah, blah, you'll get this and this and this. And like, trust me, you've got to take these medications to fix it all. Like what? That model of care, that philosophy of health, you're almost basically saying to the human on the other side, you're fucking retarded. You're weak, you're weak, retarded and you can't do anything by yourself. You have no power, take this pill because it'll fix you. Trust in the pill, trust in the man -made thing and come back to see me when you need. Like what kind of fucking care is that? Anyway, that's a different video. I'm glad I came into physiotherapy. I'm glad it turned out the way it did. If you want to pick an industry, stop overthinking it. Be critical about who you are, how you look, what you want to be, who you want to be and just put yourself in a position to succeed. So with that onwards and upwards and here's to your success.
